# sampleSizeCalc

> Sample Size Calculator for Clinical Research

A comprehensive R package for sample size determination across **39 design
combinations**: experimental trials (superiority / non-inferiority /
equivalence), observational studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional),
diagnostic accuracy studies (estimation, testing, comparison, AUC), and
complex designs (cluster RCT, Simon two-stage, bioequivalence, ordered
outcomes, prediction models, interrupted time series).

Every result displays the formula in plain text and LaTeX, a calculation
process, and literature references in the default R console output.
Parameter roles and methodological hints are included where available.

## Installation

```{r installation, eval = FALSE}
devtools::install_github("portos-wang/sampleSizeCalc")
# or from a local source
devtools::install_local("path/to/Sample_Size_Calc")
```

## Quick start: clinical study planning

These are teaching protocols with illustrative clinical inputs. In a real
study, document compatible evidence for the expected effects, variability,
prevalence, and margins; a citation for the formula does not establish
those clinical assumptions. The
[English](https://portos-wang.github.io/Sample_Size_Calc/articles/sampleSizeCalc-guide-en.html)
and [Chinese](https://portos-wang.github.io/Sample_Size_Calc/articles/sampleSizeCalc-guide-zh.html)
guides expand 52 scenarios into population, endpoint, parameter, design,
and recruitment decisions.

**Scenario 1 — Antihypertensive RCT (continuous endpoint).** A blinded,
1:1 parallel trial enrolls adults aged 40–75 with stable background
therapy. The primary endpoint is baseline minus week-12 systolic BP,
using the same averaged seated-reading protocol at both visits. Assume
mean reductions of 10 mmHg with placebo and 12 mmHg with study treatment,
with change-score SD 3 mmHg, two-sided alpha 0.05, and power 80%.
The relevant SD is for the change score, not baseline BP. The decision
is how many independent patients with complete endpoints are required.

```{r scenario-1}
library(sampleSizeCalc)

# design x task x outcome
trial_mean <- calculate("rct", "test", "mean",
  mean1 = 10, mean2 = 12, sd = 3
)
trial_mean
```

This requires `r trial_mean$n_per_group` complete patients per arm. If
10% are expected to lack the primary endpoint, plan
`r ceiling(trial_mean$n_per_group / 0.9)` recruits per arm
(`r 2 * ceiling(trial_mean$n_per_group / 0.9)` total); this additional
allowance is not included in the displayed RCT result.

**Scenario 2 — *H. pylori* eradication RCT (binary endpoint).** Adults
with confirmed infection are randomized to two 14-day regimens. Define
eradication by a standardized post-treatment breath test in a fixed
follow-up window, with prespecified rules for invalid tests, rescue
treatment, and missing assessments. Assume cure rates of 85% and 70%,
with independent groups, two-sided alpha 0.05, and power 80%. Evidence
for these rates should match treatment history and local resistance
patterns; symptomatic improvement is not the eradication endpoint.

```{r scenario-2}
trial_prop <- calculate("rct", "test", "proportion",
  p1 = 0.85, p2 = 0.70
)
trial_prop
```

The result is `r trial_prop$n_per_group` patients per arm,
`r trial_prop$total_n` total. Endpoint completeness of 90% would require
`r ceiling(trial_prop$n_per_group / 0.9)` recruits per arm, alongside the
prespecified analysis and missing-data strategy.

**Scenario 3 — Test versus reference formulation (bioequivalence).**
Eligible healthy adults are randomized to AB or BA in a two-period
crossover study. Evaluate one prespecified log-transformed PK endpoint,
such as AUC, with standardized sampling and a justified washout period.
Assume within-subject CV 25%, expected geometric mean ratio 1.0,
acceptance limits 0.80–1.25, one-sided alpha 0.05, and target power 80%.
CV should come from compatible crossover data for the same PK endpoint;
additional co-primary PK endpoints require their own planning.

```{r scenario-3}
be_trial <- calculate("bioequivalence", "equivalence", "mean", cv = 0.25)
be_trial
```

This needs `r be_trial$n_required` complete subjects per sequence,
`r be_trial$total_n` total, each completing both periods. With 10%
incomplete follow-up, a balanced recruitment plan is
`r 2 * ceiling(be_trial$n_required / 0.9)` subjects.

**Scenario 4 — Diagnostic sensitivity in a colorectal referral clinic.**
Consecutively enroll symptomatic or high-risk patients referred for
colonoscopy, collect the index-test specimen before reference assessment,
and keep the positive threshold fixed. Assume sensitivity 85%, a 95%
CI half-width of 0.05, and disease prevalence 20% in this referral setting.
Prevalence converts confirmed-case requirements into screening capacity;
it is not the test sensitivity and need not match community prevalence.
Plan specificity separately if it is also a primary objective.

```{r scenario-4}
diag_precision <- calculate("diagAccuracy", "estimate", "proportion",
  prob = 0.85, d = 0.05, prevalence = 0.2
)
diag_precision
```

The requirement is `r diag_precision$target_state_cases_needed` confirmed
cases, with an expectation-based screening total of
`r diag_precision$total_subjects_to_screen`. A 90% probability of enough
cases instead requires `r screen_required(diag_precision$target_state_cases_needed, 0.2, beta = 0.1)`
complete participants under the binomial prevalence assumption. Incomplete
reference examinations need additional operational allowance.

**Scenario 5 — Diabetes prevalence in a defined older population.**
A district survey samples eligible residents aged 65 years or older from
an explicit population frame. Apply the same disease-ascertainment
protocol to each participant. For teaching, assume prevalence 30% and
seek a 95% CI absolute half-width of 5 percentage points; this is precision
estimation, so no between-group difference or target power is specified.
Cluster sampling and nonresponse require separate adjustments.

```{r scenario-5}
survey <- calculate("singleProportion", p = 0.30, precision = 0.05)
survey
```

Obtain `r survey$n_required` valid records; at a 90% response rate, invite
about `r ceiling(survey$n_required / 0.9)` people before any design-effect
adjustment.

**Scenario 6 — Precision of a continuous biomarker's AUC.** Select
reference-confirmed cases and clinically comparable non-cases in equal
numbers, using a frozen score and one observation per patient. Assume
AUC 0.80 and a 95% CI half-width of 0.10 under a binormal variance model.
The quota sample estimates discrimination; it does not directly estimate
population prevalence. Because this design is unambiguous, `task` and
`outcome` can be omitted:

```{r scenario-6}
auc_precision <- calculate("diagAUC", auc = 0.80, d = 0.10,
  ratio = 1, var_method = "binormal"
)
auc_precision
```

Plan `r auc_precision$target_state_cases_needed` cases and the same number
of non-cases, each contributing a complete score and reference result.

Illegal combinations error with the list of legal ones. The
[English guide](https://portos-wang.github.io/Sample_Size_Calc/articles/sampleSizeCalc-guide-en.html)
and [Chinese guide](https://portos-wang.github.io/Sample_Size_Calc/articles/sampleSizeCalc-guide-zh.html)
cover design choices, parameters, formulas, and worked clinical examples.
The [regression tests](https://github.com/portos-wang/Sample_Size_Calc/tree/master/tests/testthat)
check sample sizes against published examples.

## Legacy API (silently compatible)

All 17 pre-3.0 keywords keep working with identical results:

```{r legacy-api}
sample_size_calculator("twoMeans", mean1 = 10, mean2 = 12, sd = 3)  # 37/group
sample_size_calculator("survival", hr = 0.7)                        # 247 events
```

## Result object

`calculate()` returns a `sample_size_result` S3 object. Printing the object
(or calling `print()`) displays the design, sample size, and all four
report components:

| Report component | Console label | Result field |
|---|---|---|
| Plain-text formula | `Formula (plain text)` | `formula` |
| LaTeX source | `Formula (LaTeX)` | `formula_latex` |
| Calculation process | `Calculation process` | `calculation_steps` (also `calculation`) |
| Literature sources | `Reference` | `reference` |

The same reporting components are available through
`sample_size_calculator()`. Assigning a result to a variable stores it;
print that variable to display the report. `summary()` additionally shows
all input parameters, classification axes, and recorded adjustments.
`plot()` provides the supported visual diagnostics.

```{r result-object}
res <- calculate("rct", "test", "mean", mean1 = 10, mean2 = 12, sd = 3)
summary(res)
```

You can also extract the report components for a protocol or manuscript:

```{r report-fields, eval = FALSE}
res$formula
cat(res$formula_latex)
cat(res$calculation_steps, sep = "\n")
cat(res$reference)
```

The R console displays LaTeX as copyable source. In an R Markdown document,
use `cat(res$formula_latex)` in a chunk with `results = "asis"` to typeset it.
See the [reporting guide](https://portos-wang.github.io/Sample_Size_Calc/articles/result-reporting.html) for an executed
example and instructions in English and Chinese.

## Study designs (family overview)

| Family | Designs |
|---|---|
| Trials | `rct` (test/NI/superiority/equivalence x mean/proportion/survival), `paired` (mean/proportion), `rctSingleArm`, `crossover`, `bioequivalence`, `singleArmPhaseII` (Simon optimal/minimax, A'Hern) |
| Observational | `cohort` (proportion/rate), `caseControl`, `caseControlMatched`, `crosstab` |
| Diagnostic | `diagAccuracy` (estimate/test/dual-endpoint), `diagAccuracyCompare` (test/NI/equivalence), `diagAUC`, `diagAUCCompare` (test/NI/equivalence), `diagLR` |
| Estimation | `singleProportion`, `singleMean`, `singleCorrelation` |
| Complex | `clusterRCT`, `steppedWedge`, `kappa`, `twoOrdinal`, `predictiveModel`, `its` (experimental) |

## Literature

Methods are anchored to primary sources, with worked examples from the
reference literature used as automated numeric test benchmarks:

- Zhou, Obuchowski & McClish (2011). *Statistical Methods in Diagnostic
  Medicine* (2nd ed.), Wiley - diagnostic module.
- Machin, Campbell, Tan & Tan (2018). *Sample Sizes for Clinical, Laboratory
  and Epidemiology Studies* (4th ed.), Wiley - trial/complex designs.
- Hajian-Tilaki (2014). *J Biomed Informatics* 48:193-204 - diagnostic
  formulas.
- Akoglu (2022). *Turkish J Emergency Medicine* 22(4):177-185 - diagnostic
  comparisons and dual-endpoint strategy.
- Bhardwaj et al. (2024). *J Family Med Prim Care* 13(7):2555-2561 -
  prevalence studies and dropout adjustment.
- Plus the original methods: Schoenfeld (1983), Fleiss et al. (1980),
  Casagrande et al. (1978), Schlesselman (1982), Dupont (1988), Connor
  (1987), Hanley & McNeil (1982/1983), Buderer (1996), Simon (1989),
  A'Hern (2001), Whitehead (1993), Peduzzi et al. (1996), Schuirmann (1987).

papers for each design (listed in every result's `reference` field) along
with the package:

```bibtex
@software{sampleSizeCalc,
  title = {sampleSizeCalc: Sample Size Calculator for Clinical Research},
  author = {Portos (Yishan) Wang and Bingxin Cai},
  organization = {Gansu Provincial Maternity and Child-care Hospital (Gansu Provincial Central Hospital)},
  year = {2026},
  version = {3.1.1},

}
```
